title: Salt and light
hookLine: ye are the salt of the earth, the light of the world (Matthew 5:13–16)
tomorrow: what if you remember a fight halfway through a prayer?

lines: A GOOD THING, AND A PHOTO.
cards: Somebody did a good thing on Saturday: picked up trash on a trail, served at a shelter, sat with a neighbor. Now there's a photo, and a question. Post it, or not?
Half of it feels like bragging; half of it might get someone else out there. That's yesterday's question, Zoe's question, and an old one.
Matthew says Jesus saw the crowds, went up into a mountain, sat down, and began to teach. A few lines in, he walks straight into it.

teach.h: YE ARE THE SALT OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: Right after the blessings that open the sermon, Jesus tells his listeners who they are. "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?"
Salt does its work by disappearing into the food. You taste the meal, not the salt.

teach.h: A CITY ON A HILL CANNOT BE HID.
teach.b: Then the opposite picture: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." Nobody lights a lamp, he says, and puts it under a bushel, a basket; it goes on a stand to light the whole house.
Then the line: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Look where the credit goes.

teach.h: SEEN, SO THE PRAISE GOES PAST YOU.
teach.b: The good works are seen, but the praise isn't meant to land on the one who did them. It passes through.
That's the teaching: Christians read salt and light as a calling for ordinary followers, not a few heroes, to be useful and visible in the world in a way that points past themselves to God.

teach.h: YE ARE, NOT YE SHOULD BE.
teach.b: One to tell a friend: he says ye are, not ye should be.
He tells them what they already are. And hold this one: a few lines later, the same sermon says do your giving in secret. Both are in the same sermon, and you'll hear how they fit.

how: Christians read the salt and light sayings (Matthew 5:13–16) as a calling to visible good works that point to God; the passage is read in churches and often taught at confirmations and commissioning services.

o: staying plain and humble, never standing out at all
keeping your faith private so that no one notices it
being useful and seen, so others see good and praise God

games.q: the sermon's two pictures: tap the pairs.
p: the basket the lamp doesn't go under
seen, so the Father is glorified

s: 'let your light shine' means take credit for your good deeds
the point is that people glorify your Father which is in heaven, not the doer.
in the sermon, nobody lights a lamp to hide it under a bushel
it goes on a stand and gives light to all that are in the house.
salt and light are warnings Jesus gives to outsiders
they're what he tells his listeners they already are: ye are.

games.q: your book club raised money for a family whose house burned, and the local paper wants a story. what does salt and light suggest?
o: do the story, and keep the focus on the family's need and the help, not the club.
turn it down; a good deed loses its worth the moment anyone sees it.
do it, and make sure every member's name is printed so each one is thanked.
games.why: light is meant to be seen, so others see the good and give glory past you. the spotlight goes on the work, not the workers.

practice: Choose one small good thing to do in the open this week: holding a door, thanking someone by name in front of others, picking up litter where people walk. Plan the place and the time in one sentence.
Then sit, and let it be ordinary.

wordCard.voice: Salt and light: Jesus's two pictures of his listeners, one that disappears into the meal and one that can't be hid.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 5:13: the salt of the earth.

carryVoice: The line to keep: salt and light, seen so the praise goes past you. The sermon has started; see you tomorrow.
